# Polished Academic Version

Understanding the role of motivation in student engagement with laboratory skill education is fundamental to enhancing learning outcomes and academic achievement. Physical science laboratories serve as experiential learning environments where students develop higher-order conceptual understanding and practical competencies. Student attitudes toward these laboratory experiences significantly influence the effectiveness of skill acquisition. 

The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a rapid transition to alternative pedagogical approaches, with computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) emerging as a viable medium for skill training and experimentation under lockdown constraints. However, widespread VL adoption has been hindered by limited awareness and insufficient familiarity among both educators and students. 

This study investigates the key motivational factors affecting VL efficacy in developing students' laboratory skills and competencies. Survey data were collected using three validated instruments: the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) scale, a self-reported questionnaire assessing extrinsic factors, and a teacher perception scale regarding VL implementation. Data analysis employed independent sample t-tests and automatic linear modeling (LINEAR) to identify significant relationships.

The findings reveal several critical insights. First, animated graphic learning materials in VLs demonstrated significantly greater impact on students' intrinsic motivation compared to traditional e-book formats. Second, teacher involvement proved essential in elevating student motivation levels for conducting virtual laboratory experiments. Third, extended or repeated engagement with VL experiments positively correlated with improved student laboratory performance, suggesting that increased exposure enhances skill development and learning outcomes.

These results have important implications for the design and implementation of virtual laboratory environments in science education.
